module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 253

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/253](https://www.erdosproblems.com/253)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos253

open scoped Topology

/-- The predicate that `a : ℕ → ℕ` is a strictly monotone sequence such that every infinite
arithmetic progression contains infinitely many integers that are the sum of distinct $a_i$s. -/
@[inline]
def RepresentsAPs (a : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop :=
    StrictMono a ∧ ∀ l, l.IsAPOfLength ⊤ → (subsetSums (Set.range a) ∩ l).Infinite

/--
Let $a_1 < a_2 < \dotsc$ be an infinite sequence of positive integers such that
$\frac{a_{i+1}}{a_i} \to 1$. If every arithmetic progression contains infinitely many
integers which are the sum of distinct $a_i$ then every sufficiently large integer is
the sum of distinct $a_i$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/1268917deaaaa0d674f651287027baa26cea9920/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos253.lean#L699"]
theorem erdos_253 : ¬ ∀ a : ℕ → ℕ, 0 < a 0 →
    RepresentsAPs a → (Filter.atTop.Tendsto (fun n ↦ (a <| n + 1 : ℝ) / a n) (𝓝 1)) →
      subsetSums (Set.range a) ∈ Filter.cofinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos253

reformulations.difference: Erdős’s original formulation on p. 345 requires every arithmetic progression to contain at least one integer representable as a sum of distinct terms. The Lean helper requires infinitely many such integers in every infinite AP.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every tail of an infinite AP is itself an infinite AP. Applying the nonempty-intersection condition to arbitrarily distant tails gives an unbounded, hence infinite, intersection with the original AP. The converse is immediate. Proved as Review253.all_AP_nonempty_iff_infinite and Review253.representsAPs_iff_primary in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: The statement expresses positivity through `0 < a 0` together with strict monotonicity, and expresses eventual representability through membership in `Filter.cofinite`. It records the known disproof by negating the universal implication.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Strict monotonicity gives `a 0 ≤ a n`, so the positivity condition is equivalent to positivity of every term. On ℕ, cofinite membership is equivalent to `∃ N, ∀ n ≥ N, n ∈ subsetSums (Set.range a)`. Together with the AP equivalence, this identifies the proposition with the negation of Erdős’s original conjecture, whose disproof he explicitly records on p. 346. The full equivalence is proved as Review253.negative_iff_primary; equivalence with existence of a counterexample having infinitely many unrepresentable integers is also proved.

sources_consulted: P. Erdős, “On the representation of large integers as sums of distinct summands taken from a fixed set,” Acta Arithmetica 7 (1962), especially pp. 345–346: https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1961-18.pdf

J. W. S. Cassels, “On the representation of integers as the sums of distinct summands taken from a fixed set,” Acta Scientiarum Mathematicarum 21 (1960), Theorem II, p. 112, and its proof, pp. 122–124: https://acta.bibl.u-szeged.hu/13906/1/math_021_fasc_003_004_111-124.pdf
review.notes:
No mathematical defects found in either declaration. Checked that infinite APs have positive common difference, sums use distinct terms, the empty sum only adds the harmless value 0, and the ratio uses real division with positive denominators. The hypotheses are satisfiable, as verified for a n = n + 1.

The main erdosproblems.com page and forum were blocked by Cloudflare despite descriptive User-Agent headers. The mathematical comparison therefore used the original Erdős and Cassels papers. The community database independently records problem 253 as disproved with a Lean proof, agreeing with the file.

Compiled the exact cited external proof and a bridge proving the repository’s proposition from it. `#print axioms` reports only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound—no sorryAx or custom axioms. Experiments and proof checks are in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, linked-proof-check.lean, and proof-bridge.lean.
